Sample text:
---
When the city put a bench at the top of Mercer Hill, my father wrote to complain that it faced the wrong way. He had a point. In one direction you could see the harbor, the grain elevators, and, on a clear day, the white scar on Dunley Island where a hotel had slid into the sea. In the other direction you could see the back of a pharmacy. The bench faced the pharmacy.

He enclosed a photograph and a self-addressed envelope. Three weeks later a woman from Public Works called to say the bench had been turned around.

“Just like that?” he asked.

“Four bolts,” she said.

He was delighted. For years he had voted, attended meetings, signed petitions. Here was a photograph he had taken on a Wednesday producing, by the following month, a change in the physical arrangement of the world. He walked up Mercer Hill to inspect it. An old woman was sitting on the bench backward, her shoes planted in the flower bed, her arms folded across the backrest.

“Better view on this side,” he said, pointing.

“I know what the harbor looks like.”

He stood there a moment. The pharmacy had blue bins, a drainpipe, and a steel door with a square of wired glass.

“What are you looking at, then?”

“My son comes out at three.”

It was ten to three. My father sat beside her, facing the harbor. A tug pushed two barges past the elevators. He tried to decide whether to tell her he was responsible for the bench. Before he could make up his mind, the steel door opened and a man in a white coat came out carrying a banana and a paperback. He saw the woman, held up the banana in greeting, and sat on an overturned crate to read.

“Doesn’t he come over?” my father asked.

“He’s on his break,” she said, as if this were an odd question, which it was.

My father told this story often. Depending on his audience, it demonstrated either that the city was unusually responsive or that a person ought to mind his business. When he told it to children, he made the banana a different fruit each time. My niece once interrupted to say that nobody held up a bowl of cherries in one hand while carrying an open book in the other, and he conceded the point.

Years later, after he died, my brother and I went up Mercer Hill. We were supposed to be choosing a place to scatter his ashes, a task for which he had left instructions of magnificent uselessness: *Somewhere outdoors.*

The bench was gone. In its place stood a metal cabinet marked TRAFFIC SIGNAL CONTROL. The pharmacy was now a dance school. Through the wired glass we could see a red cardigan hanging on a hook.

My brother set the cardboard box on the cabinet and bent to tie his shoe. Immediately a voice behind us said, “You can’t leave that there.”

It belonged to a little girl in a black leotard, holding the steel door open with her hip.

“We’re not leaving it,” I said.

“Because people put drinks there and then they blow over and the straws go down the drain.”

“Do they?”

She pointed. There were indeed several striped straws behind the grate.

My brother picked up the box. “What should people do?”

“Hold their drinks.”

The door shut. We stood looking at the spot where she had been, and then my brother began to laugh. He had our father’s laugh, which started so quietly you often mistook it for a cough and offered him water just as he got going.

We took the ashes down to the harbor. At low tide there was a little beach beside the ferry slip, and we waited there for a family to finish collecting shells. My brother rolled his trousers to the knee. I held his belt while he waded out, because the stones were slick and because neither of us wanted to explain to our mother that we had dropped Dad in with the packaging.

It went fine. Some ashes floated; most sank. A ferry backed out of its slip with a shudder that traveled through the soles of my feet. My brother came ashore and dried his legs with his socks, thereby creating a problem he had not anticipated.

On the walk home he stopped at the pharmacy on King Street to buy another pair. I waited outside with the empty box. After a while the automatic doors parted and he emerged, wearing his new socks and carrying, in addition to the old ones, two bottles of water and a banana.

I’m aware that the banana is a bit much. If I were making this up I’d give him chewing gum, or nothing at all. But he came through those doors, saw me on the curb, and raised that banana over his head, and for once in my life I was looking exactly the right way.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A crafted, quietly comic family story with a clear narrative arc from a civic-minded father’s small victory to his children’s remembrance of him.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and affectionate, letting grief arrive through practical details rather than grand declarations: slick stones, unusable instructions, damp socks, and a banana held aloft. Its humor doesn’t undercut the loss; it makes the father’s habits and the siblings’ tenderness feel lived-in. The story invites the reader to notice how people can face the same place for entirely different reasons, and how a gesture can become meaningful through repetition and memory.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds ordinary public space—a bench, a pharmacy door, a harbor—as a meeting point for competing needs and private attachments. It favors small, concrete interventions and objects over abstract claims: four bolts turn the bench, a son’s break shapes an old woman’s view, and a banana becomes an inherited greeting. Grief is present but handled through sibling banter and bodily logistics, ending with the narrator recognizing that, this time, they were looking in the right direction.

## Evidence line
> But he came through those doors, saw me on the curb, and raised that banana over his head, and for once in my life I was looking exactly the right way.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The piece is coherent and distinctive, with recurring objects and a carefully earned emotional resolution that make its chosen blend of humor, attention, and understated grief especially legible.
